paragraphs.heading: The puzzle
paragraphs.text: Picture yourself on a game show in front of three doors. A car waits behind one door and a goat stands behind each of the others. You choose a door, and the host, who knows where everything is, opens a different door to show a goat. He then asks whether you would like to move to the remaining closed door instead.

paragraphs.heading: The surprising answer
paragraphs.text: Savant answered that the player should switch. Under the usual assumptions, switching wins the car with probability 2/3, while sticking with the first door wins only 1/3 of the time. The answer feels so wrong that it is called a veridical paradox: a result that can look absurd and yet can be shown to be true.

paragraphs.heading: The rules the host follows
paragraphs.text: The answer rests on a model of how the host behaves and where the prize goes. He always opens a door the player did not pick, always shows a goat rather than the car, and always offers the switch. The car is placed at random, and if the player has picked the car, the host chooses at random which goat door to open. Change these assumptions and the chance of winning by switching can change too.

paragraphs.heading: Why switching wins
paragraphs.text: At the start, the car sits behind one of the two doors you did not pick two times out of three. If your first pick was a goat, the host has to reveal the other goat, so switching lands you on the car. If your first pick was the car, switching loses. So a player who switches wins exactly when the first pick was a goat, which has probability 2/3.

paragraphs.heading: Where intuition goes wrong
paragraphs.text: Most people decide that switching cannot matter, since the car seems equally likely to be behind either closed door. That would be right if the host picked a door to open at random, but he does not. The door he opens depends on the door you chose, so independence does not hold. Another way to see it: the host is in effect letting you trade your one door for both of the others, and that pair holds the car with probability 2/3.

paragraphs.heading: A million doors
paragraphs.text: Savant suggested imagining 1,000,000 doors instead of three to make the answer feel natural. You pick door #1. The host, who knows where the prize is and always avoids it, then opens every door except door #777,777. Faced with that, you would move to the one door he left shut without much hesitation.

paragraphs.heading: A famous argument
paragraphs.text: After the problem appeared in Parade, about 10,000 readers wrote in, close to 1,000 of them with PhDs, and most said Savant was wrong. Many people kept rejecting the answer even after seeing explanations, simulations and formal proofs. The mathematician Paul Erdős stayed unconvinced until someone showed him a computer simulation that produced the predicted result. Steve Selvin had written to the American Statistician in 1975 about a puzzle based on the show Let's Make a Deal, and gave it the name Monty Hall problem in a later letter.
